# Build and Compile Delegation Troubleshooting Tree

Investigate Build and Compile delegation issues through a single CI run first, not by reading configuration. During migration, the traces most likely to remain are indications that modules, tasks, or switches exist; these traces show that an entry point can be found, but not that the build, compile, and test stages are connected as expected.

At a minimum, the team on site should be able to identify the entry point, source revision, build output, compile output, and test report for the same run. If any item is missing, simply record the gap; do not mark that run as confirmed. JEX-213 provides navigation for this check: the to-do item in the card explicitly requires confirming whether delegation takes effect in a real CI run. The existence of a configuration file cannot substitute for run results.

## Start with the Report

First check whether the report contains the test entries to be verified in this run. Here, “contains” means that the test framework actually generated report records, not that test files exist in the code directory or that the build log printed a module name.

```text
Obtain a CI run
│
├─ No run entry point, or the run is no longer accessible
│  └─ Stop: obtain a traceable run; do not infer results from local configuration
│
├─ A run entry point exists, but there is no build output
│  └─ Stop: cannot distinguish between the entry point not starting and logs not being retained
│
├─ Build output exists, but there is no compile-stage record
│  └─ Save the build output and the location of the gap, and check whether this entry point actually reached compilation
│
├─ The compile stage has records, but the test report does not contain the target test
│  └─ Check test selection, skip status, and tag conditions first
│
└─ The test report contains the target test
   ├─ Build, compilation, and testing come from the same source revision
   │  └─ Continue comparing the stage boundaries in the three sets of output
   └─ The revision is inconsistent or not recorded
      └─ Stop: the three pieces of evidence cannot be combined into a single verification
```

Save “build output” and “compile-stage records” separately. The former only indicates that the CI entry point started processing the module; the latter is what determines whether that entry point triggered compilation. The test report is a third piece of evidence: it answers whether tests were actually discovered and executed after compilation. The existence of all three pieces does not automatically constitute evidence that delegation took effect. They must come from the same run, with no break in the sequence.

If a run leaves only a final success or failure status, with no stage output, do not interpret that final status as successful compilation. Success may result from the target test not being selected, and failure may occur before compilation. In this case, retain the final status and the available range of output, then rerun through a CI entry point that can retain stage evidence. Do not fill in missing stages using a report from another unrelated run.

## First Identify Which Stage Is Missing

When the build stage has not started at all, investigate whether the CI entry point for this run received the module, not `SecondTest.java`. This branch does not require changing test selection first. If the run entry point cannot be located, or there is no source revision, stop here; any subsequent source-code comparison will have no corresponding reference.

When the build has started but the compile stage cannot be found, focus on whether the output contains an explicit compilation action or an explicit reason for skipping it. Do not treat “the build task finished” as “compilation has been delegated.” If the output provides only a summary status, record that it covers only the build entry point, and wait for a run containing stage information. Adjusting tags, disable markers, or assertions first is not recommended at this point, because there is no evidence yet that the test discovery stage has been reached.

When the compile stage exists but the target test has not entered the report, shift the investigation to test selection. The designated file to check is:

`junit5-maven-consumer/src/test/java/com/example/project/SecondTest.java`

This file is in the `com.example.project` package, and the following direct dependencies are visible at the top of the file:

```java
import static org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.assertEquals;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Disabled;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Tag;
```

Start with two small checks here: first, confirm whether the target test is still in this package and path in the source revision for this run; second, confirm whether `Disabled` or `Tag` is actually applied to the selected test or an adjacent object. An import is only a clue for checking back; it does not mean that the test is disabled or tagged, or that `assertEquals` has executed on this run's path.

If an actual disable marker is confirmed, the absence of the target test from the report does not indicate that Build and Compile delegation failed; it only indicates that the current selection conditions did not allow this test to execute. Retain the marker's location, the skipped or absent status in the report, and the selection conditions for this run. Do not simply remove the disable marker to obtain a report entry.

If tag-based selection is confirmed, first compare the selection conditions used by the run with the test's actual tags. If the tags do not match, record the issue as a test selection issue, not a compile delegation issue. If the tags match but the report entry is still missing, go back and check whether the compile output and test discovery output belong to the same run.

If the test is neither actually disabled nor excluded by a tag mismatch, but still does not appear, continue checking whether the report covers only some modules or some test engines. Do not directly attribute the absence to delegation here either: the available evidence only supports confirming that the report is missing entries; it cannot replace observation of the discovery process.

## Examine Delegation Boundaries Only After a Report Is Available

When the report contains the target test, arrange the three pieces of evidence chronologically: when the build entry point started processing the module, when compilation generated records, and when the test entered the report. Do not label the relationship between these three stages first. First check whether they come from the same source revision, belong to the same CI run, and are free of output mixed in from another retry or cache.

If both build and compilation are visible in the same run, and the test report also contains the target test, this run can serve as candidate evidence for checking delegation. Candidate evidence does not mean discrepancies can be ignored: if the tests listed in the report come from a different revision, or the build output does not clearly correspond to this module, the inconsistencies must still be marked in the record.

If build and testing are visible, but there is no compilation evidence between them, do not infer from successful testing that compilation was delegated. The tests may have used existing artifacts, or those artifacts may have been prepared by another unrecorded step. Maintain the assessment “compile stage unconfirmed” until verifiable compile records are provided for the same run.

If build, compilation, and testing are all visible, but the test result is a failure, first document the failure details separately from the stage boundaries. A failed result shows that testing reached the reporting stage; it does not by itself establish whether the delegation relationship is correct or incorrect. Include the observation in delegation troubleshooting only when the output before and after the failure shows that a stage was not triggered, was skipped, or occurred in a different run.

## The Old Check Sequence Is No Longer Enough

Earlier records tended to start with Maven consumer files and configuration. This approach is still useful, but only for narrowing the scope of inspection. The sequence now starts by pinning down one actual run, then checking back against files to explain gaps in the report.

This adjustment also retains a common counterexample: the configuration already includes the expected module, yet the CI run provides no report for the target test. In this case, do not mark it as passed just because the configuration looks complete; continue distinguishing between a missing compile stage, test selection not matching, and insufficient report coverage. Conversely, seeing a single test failure is not enough to directly conclude that there is a configuration or delegation issue.

In the card history, JEX-213 was handed over to the person handling on-site integration testing on 2025-09-29, and moved from To Do to In Progress on 2025-10-06. These actions indicate that someone has taken ownership of the check, not that a run has passed. Subsequent supporting evidence should be attached to the same actual CI run, rather than merely appending status changes.

## Stop Points When Collecting Evidence

In all of the following cases, stop at the current branch; do not expand the work into source-code changes:

- Only configuration files or a directory structure exist, with no traceable CI run;
- The build log and test report cannot be tied to the same source revision;
- A final status exists, but a key stage among build, compilation, and testing is missing;
- The target test has not entered the report, and `Disabled`, `Tag`, or the selection conditions have not yet been checked;
- The report comes from another retry, while the compile output comes from the original run.

The stop-point record should include the available run entry point, the categories of output saved, which stage is missing, and which item needs to be supplied next time. # Random Parameter Injection Decision

This record originally did not treat the path as indicating implementation ownership, and that tradeoff is retained. What later needed correction were several short phrases that could easily be read as “the problem has already been located.” Random parameter injection is still documented here as an anomaly for a specific usage pattern: there is a test location that can be looked up, a ticket requiring two types of samples to be retained, and several inference boundaries that must not be crossed. It is not yet a description of the parameter mechanism, much less an overall conclusion about migration scope.

The original wording left the issue open in two directions: do random parameters enter the context during test setup or during parameter parsing, and are failed invocations related to the condition implied by the name BaseClass? It was right not to rush to attribution at the time. The real problem is not that these two question marks exist, but that readers can easily fill in the answer themselves from the filename, directory name, and assertion imports.

The old clues are retained below, while the parts that can and cannot be established are separated.

## The old entry point is unchanged

The current lookup entry point is:

`junit5-mockito-extension/src/test/java/com/example/mockito/MockitoExtensionInBaseClassTest.java`

The declaration that can be located directly is:

```java
class MockitoExtensionInBaseClassTest {
```

The file header belongs to the `com.example.mockito` package and contains three static imports:

```java
import static org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.assertEquals;
import static org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.assertNotNull;
import static org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.assertNotSame;
```

These items have a stable purpose in this record: they allow later reviewers to begin verification from the same Java test class. The class name aids searching; the package name helps confirm the location; and the assertion names help find checkpoints in the file that may carry the result forward. That is all.

The path being under `junit5-mockito-extension` does not mean that this module is responsible for generating random parameters. The test file's use of assertions does not mean that parameter behavior is determined by JUnit itself. The class name contains BaseClass, which likewise does not mean that the existence of a parent class or inheritance chain is already known. The current location provides no `extends` declaration, nor a parameter generator, parameter parser, extension registration statement, or caller path. In the earlier draft, these gaps were simply unresolved items; it is now explicitly required not to treat them as missing information that can be filled in from names.

This is particularly true of `assertNotSame`. This assertion does indicate that the test author cares that two objects should not be the same object, but it cannot by itself prove that the objects came from random injection. The objects being different may result from test setup or from another construction path that is not shown. If this is translated as “random parameters have been verified,” the checking tool is being misrepresented as the source of the parameters.

`assertEquals` and `assertNotNull` are clues of the same kind. Equality, non-nullness, and being different objects are properties the test may check; they are not execution paths available on this page. If a future reference shows how parameter values reach the test method, it can be added beside the corresponding sample. Without that reference, we can only retain the current local observation.

## What this record actually preserves

There are four objects in the history that are easiest to confuse. They were originally distinguished by context; they are now fixed separately.

**Requirement name.** Random parameter injection is the object name in this migration history. It lets readers find discussions of the same kind, but does not explain where the parameters are generated, how they are passed, when they are bound, or at which layer they fail. The name is not an implementation description.

**Test observation point.** `MockitoExtensionInBaseClassTest.java` is the currently reviewable location. This location can serve as the anchor for subsequent inspection of test content and actual references. The observation point is not ownership. Writing “handle the problem here” when the intended meaning is “see the problem here” conflates the investigation entry point with the implementation location.

**Result comparison.** The local notes for JEX-216 require the visible results of a successful call and a failed call to be recorded separately. This establishes two samples that need to be retained side by side. It does not declare random parameters usable as a whole, nor does it declare them unusable as a whole.

**Migration background.** 2026.09 migration train explains why this observation entered the requirement history. It does not provide a before-and-after behavior comparison, nor does it provide any cross-module material that could be used to determine the scope of impact. Migration background cannot automatically become fault attribution.

Once these four types of objects are separated, subsequent new material should first be classified as belonging to one of them. A test output belongs to the result comparison; a newly found reference may supplement the test observation point; only an explicit change record may affect the interpretation of the migration background. If material cannot bridge the gap between objects, do not use it to build that bridge. This does not mean leaving the matter suspended forever; it means avoiding a local anomaly becoming a conclusion about a global mechanism through retelling.

## Successful and failed calls

The observation when JEX-216 were created was “an anomaly in a specific usage pattern of Random parameter.” “Specific usage pattern” is the scope term for this record and must not be omitted from summaries, review comments, or descriptions in subsequent cards. Writing only “random parameter anomaly” would bring unobserved usage conditions into the problem scope as well; writing only “there was one success” would expand a single sample into general recovery.

The current way of recording this is as follows.

| Sample | Content to record | Content that must not be inferred from it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Successful call | The result left by that call; the assertion or test output that records the result | All Random parameter paths are functioning normally; the failed sample is no longer valid |
| Failed call | The result left by that call; the anomalous behavior visible at the time | The anomaly has been confirmed to be caused by the Mockito extension, JUnit, or the migration |

The table does not require every addition to use the same format. It fixes only two decisions: samples must not be merged, and conclusions must not overreach. If new material provides only a successful call, add the successful call; if it provides only a failure symptom, add the failed call. When the parameter context is still absent, leaving it blank is more accurate than guessing.

Here, “visible result” is a narrowly defined term. It refers only to a result left by a call or test at the time it runs that can be reviewed afterward, such as the state checked by an assertion or a phenomenon shown in the test output. It is not a summary of quality, nor a card status, and certainly not a directory name. A result can be a valuable sample yet still be insufficient to explain the cause.

The point of placing successful and failed samples together is not to let them cancel each other out. A successful call shows that no abnormal behavior appeared in that particular call; a failed call shows that abnormal behavior occurred with that usage pattern. The coexistence of both shows precisely why they cannot first be reduced to “the feature works” or “the feature does not work”. If they are later found to come from different reference paths, the paths should be attached separately to their respective samples, rather than forcibly grouping them under the same condition to maintain a single narrative.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    state "Test entry point" as entry
    state "Successful call" as success
    state "Failed call" as failure
    state "Saved side by side" as paired
    state "Parameter context pending investigation" as pending
    [*] --> entry
    entry --> success: Successful sample
    entry --> failure: Failed sample
    success --> paired
    failure --> paired
    paired --> pending
```

This diagram does not depict success and failure as states that transition into each other. The two branches start at the test entry point, indicating only that the current material can be traced back starting from the same test class; they converge at “Saved side by side”, indicating that neither side may erase the other; they then stop at “Parameter context pending investigation”, indicating that the two results do not yet establish a parameter path.

## Several approaches to writing this that have already been abandoned

The first rejected approach was to attribute the abnormal behavior directly to the Mockito extension. It seems natural: the entry point is in `junit5-mockito-extension`, and the test class name also contains Mockito. But this actually collapses two steps of inference into one. A directory can identify a module's location; it cannot prove that the module handles the behavior. The current material does not show where the parameters enter the extension, nor does it show which part of the extension the failure occurs in, so “handled by the extension” is no longer used as the conclusion on this page.

The second rejected approach was to group the three assertion imports together as evidence of the JUnit parameter mechanism. The assertions only show that the test author is checking equality, non-nullness, or object identity. They do not show how the parameters are assembled, much less whether the failure occurs before the call enters the test, during test execution, or at the assertion stage. Presenting assertion imports as evidence of the mechanism would mistakenly lead reviewers to stop at the file header instead of examining the actual test content and references.

The third rejected interpretation is to treat BaseClass as a premise for failure. The class name does indeed contain this term, but the current material contains no superclass declaration. Even if a superclass is actually found later, it would still be necessary to confirm that relationship is relevant to the successful and failed samples. The name can be used as a file-search term, but it cannot on its own establish the fact that the “base-class scenario failed.”

The fourth rejected interpretation is to treat the migration train as the cause of the regression. 2026.09 migration train is background to this request’s history. It explains why this record needs to be preserved during the migration, but it provides neither a before-and-after comparison of the same call nor a change snippet. Without those materials, “the migration caused the anomaly” is merely a convenient narrative, not a conclusion that can be retained.

The fifth rejected interpretation is to use the completion status of JEX-216 as a substitute for a behavioral conclusion. The card moved from pending to in progress and then to complete. This action indicates that the work at the card level was marked as finished at the time; it does not indicate that all usage patterns had been verified, nor that the cause of the failure had been identified. Work status and behavioral results belong to different levels. Conflating them would make a completed card bear a technical conclusion that it never recorded.

## What to Check First During Review

Start from the full path:

`junit5-mockito-extension/src/test/java/com/example/mockito/MockitoExtensionInBaseClassTest.java`

First confirm the actual test contents and adjacent references in this version. If you can find an assertion covering a successful call or a failed call, first attribute the result to the correct sample. If you can see context related to the parameters, then determine whether it concerns test setup, parameter parsing, extension behavior, or some other location. The order cannot be reversed: visible results and references must come first, followed by discussion of causes.

The package name `com.example.mockito` is used to confirm the file location. The three static imports narrow the scope of the review. They should not be elevated into substitutes for the parameter path. The test class itself also cannot automatically be treated as a mirror of production behavior. Tests may expose object relationships, or they may only express the author’s expectations. Distinguishing between these cases still requires examining the test’s actual contents and call relationships.

This page does not expand the check into a process that traces every caller from the project root. The current item requires a stable historical entry point, not a code inspection with unlimited scope. If later materials show that the successful and failed cases are not in the same test location, the new locations should each remain beside their corresponding sample. The fact that the old entry point already exists is not a reason to force phenomena from different paths back into the same file.

## Division of Responsibilities Between the Card and This Page

JEX-216 are navigation points. The local requirement they leave behind is clear: save the successful and failed calls separately. That is why this page uses a sample comparison.

The card is not responsible for explaining the parameter-generation path, nor for determining responsibility for extension handling. Its status changes can help reconstruct how far the work had progressed at the time, but they cannot replace checking the test results and actual references. If it is necessary to prove that a fix covers more usage patterns, the results of the corresponding calls must be recorded. The card’s completion status cannot be interpreted as evidence of coverage.

This page is responsible for deciding the standard: what can serve as an entry point, what can only serve as a lead, what results must be stored separately, and which attributions are not to be used for now. It does not generate more samples for JEX-216, nor does it fill in parameter mechanisms that do not appear in the test file.

The adjacent DOC-26 stores materials for the Ant starter calculator result. The two documents are near each other on the same migration train and can guide each other; they discuss different subjects. This page does not move calculator results over to explain random parameters, nor does it use Random parameter injection to add implementation attribution to the other result.

## Current decision

After this round of review, retain and implement the following decisions:

1. Random parameter injection continues to be maintained on this page as an “anomalous record of a specific usage pattern,” and is not elevated to a judgment about a global parameter mechanism.
2. `MockitoExtensionInBaseClassTest.java` is the current inspection entry point. It is used to review local test behavior and references, not to assert parameter origin, implementation ownership, or modification location.
3. Successful calls and failed calls must each leave their own visible result. Neither may represent the other.
4. `assertEquals`, `assertNotNull`, and `assertNotSame` are used only as navigation clues for test checks, and are not written up as injection sources, proof of randomness, or failure attributions.
5. BaseClass is not used as a confirmed inheritance condition unless subsequent references actually show the corresponding relationship.
6. 2026.09 migration train is retained as requirements context. This page does not, on that basis, declare that the migration caused a regression, nor does it declare that recovery has already occurred throughout the migration scope.

This does not mean that all matters are being deferred. The first four items are already-decided records of how to document things and the boundaries of interpretation: samples must be split apart, an entry point may perform only entry-point responsibilities, assertions must not go beyond their own semantics, and a local anomaly must not be expanded without evidence. What remains unconfirmed is exactly where the parameters enter the test context, whether failed calls have additional conditions, and whether successful and failed calls pass through the same reference path. These unknowns should remain in the record until specific references or results can answer them.

## Responsibility boundaries

Responsibility boundaries on this page are divided by type of judgment, not by directory name.

The person maintaining the history is responsible for preserving the relationship between the earlier assessment, the current entry point, and the two types of samples. When new results emerge, overly strong wording should be revised; a test path alone cannot settle a module-level decision.

The person checking the test entry point is responsible for confirming the actual declarations, imports, and nearby references in that version. If the conditions associated with the class name differ from those in the old draft, the relevant text should be corrected directly, rather than continuing to use the explanation that it “looks like a base-class test.”

The person providing call evidence is responsible for placing successful or failed results back with the correct samples. # Ant Calculator Results Proposal

The old draft put `FirstTest.java` near the top to give reviewers a starting point they could open. The wording at the time made it easy to read that starting point as the location of the Ant starter results; after this review, that interpretation needs to be narrowed. The file is still worth keeping in the proposal, but it only explains why the consumer test surface appeared in the earlier investigation.

The path is `junit5-maven-consumer/src/test/java/com/example/project/FirstTest.java`. The existing file header provides a small set of facts: it belongs to `com.example.project`, statically imports `assertEquals`, and imports `DisplayName` and `Tag`. These declarations support inspecting calculator-related assertions and nearby calls from the test side; they do not list Ant targets or record a particular build's artifacts in the test file.

## Assessments from the Original Draft

The original proposal split the issue into two questions: whether the calculator interface expected by the consumer was still unchanged, and whether the Ant starter had actually produced the claimed results. The first can be investigated starting near the test file; the second cannot be established from that same test source.

At the time, the preference was to review the file first. The reasoning was practical: both the old issue name and the call names pointed here, and assertions in the test directory were easier to inspect than abstract descriptions. The old draft also noted the cost of this approach: even when expected values and test annotations were visible, they were still local test expressions in the Maven consumer, not evidence of which Ant execution produced the results.

The other approach considered was to return to the repository's existing automation jobs and obtain the job, commit, and actual artifact name so they could be recorded together. The original plan did not call for changing the starter first, but for identifying the execution referred to by the result name. The old draft did not specify a job name or execution command because that material was unavailable at the time; that gap remains.

## Distinction Retained After Review

`FirstTest.java` remains a reference point for checking the consumer side. The check should answer only whether nearby assertions still concern the same kind of calculator interface, and whether the annotations and test organization explain where the old clues led. It no longer serves as proof that “the Ant starter has succeeded.”

Automation records address a different question: whether an artifact actually came from the Ant starter. Only when the job, corresponding commit, and artifact name can be included in the same record does the result name have provenance that can be discussed further. If any one of these is missing, the status should remain pending confirmation rather than being replaced by a consumer pass or failure.

These are two possible paths, not steps that must be completed in order. If the test-side check first finds that the interface shape no longer matches, that finding can be recorded as a consumer issue without inferring the Ant execution result. If a job record is found first but the artifact belongs to the Maven consumer, that only shows that the old clues conflated the result names; the test file still helps explain the source of that conflation.

## Relationship to JEX-217

JEX-217 describes the investigation in terms of the affected module scope for the Ant starter calculator, and leaves a to-do to trigger the corresponding task through the repository's existing automation jobs and record the job, commit, and actual artifact name. This connects to the second path in the old proposal, but a to-do is not a completion record and does not supply the job details missing from this proposal.

This proposal can therefore still be used to distinguish two kinds of observations: interface observations in the test file, and result observations left by automated execution. It should not be treated as the final determination for the migration train. The old draft's sentence “confirm the results from the test file first” is retained as a record of the investigation order at the time; “results” in that sentence is now limited to what was observed on the consumer test surface.

## Retraction Criteria

If later references confirm that `FirstTest.java` is only a navigation point left by the issue name and call names, retract the assumption that it was a direct location for Ant results, without deleting the file clue. If the automation job cannot provide both the commit and artifact name, the proposal will not mark the Ant starter as verified either. Conversely, even after a complete record is obtained, consumer test observations and Ant artifact records should still be stored separately so the next investigation does not merge them into a single result again.

It also stated that whether the release succeeded would be signed off separately by the corresponding maintainer. This judgment let the person closing the window verify only one record, and treated “last” as sufficient on-site evidence.

At the time, it did not separate the current entry point from the original current revision. | Split route | A separate view of the first result from `test report` | Splitting might yield only a difference in presentation |

The third row was not included in the subsequent trial plan. It was only an alternative used in review to compare whether the existing interface would be bypassed; it should not be read as an interface that had already been integrated. The original sketch made the split route sound nearly executable. In hindsight, that was also too optimistic: switching entry points had already changed what the statistics meant.

The risk recorded in JEXA-007 is that trends before and after the change to the current entry point cannot be directly subtracted from each other. This constraint changed the comparison method: rather than using aggregate trends to prove that one route was better, start from the original entry point of a real caller sample and record the input, the current revision, and the first point of divergence. The verification method proposed in JEXA-013 likewise follows the original entry point through to the current revision and stops at the first difference. “Stop” here does not mean filling in subsequent unknowns with zeros, nor does it justify declaring that the other route failed.

Another correction came later from JEXA-016. The earlier sketch assumed that as long as the report could be read, blank fields could be treated as data not collected; in fact, we first need to check whether collection and execution are enabled. Without evidence for both at the current entry point, we cannot fill in zeros. This finding invalidated the old assessment that “splitting the report is enough to locate the issue,” but that assessment remains in the sketch above because it explains why the proposal was made at the time.

If the trial is reopened, its scope should be very narrow: use only one example and one extension call sample; use the same input for the original and candidate routes, and preserve each route's version and first visible result. The comparison is not about a single green run or clearer labels, but whether readers can identify the first point where the two paths diverge. This condition is intended to prevent the candidate route from leaving a partially configured entry point, not to serve as a general process for all extension changes.

- The scope of callers in use in `extension context` had not yet been established;
- Actual users of the current revision needed to be verified through the original entry point, not inferred from trend numbers;
- When collection and execution status were unknown, blank fields in the report had no usable meaning;
- If the candidate interface bypassed the existing interface, the resulting differences could not answer the caller integration testing question.

# Mockito Entry Point Migration Index

The migration records for `junit5-mockito-extension-client-integration` are written sample by sample based on actual example and extension usage, rather than inferred from whether a directory contains new files. Each sample has its own adaptation boundary and integration feedback; similarly named side paths without the same caller are not grouped into the same batch.

We previously compared continuing to record under `launcher handoff` with splitting out `dependency graph` separately. The failure exits for the two paths differ, so the index tracks them separately: the entry location describes the destination, while the caller record describes the actual switch status.

## Three Types of Entries in the Index

Each caller retains three fields: old entry, current entry, and compatibility status.

- The old entry lists a location that can still be restored; it is not removed just because the current entry has been established;
- The current entry lists only the location that caller is preparing to use or has already used;
- The compatibility status records the adaptation conditions for switches that are not yet complete, along with the partial integration feedback received.

Entries whose callers cannot be traced remain stale. Do not use directory names, similar extension names, or a standalone release note to fill in a completed migration. The active callers for `suite selector` are still unconfirmed, so leave them in the index's unchecked items for now.

## Switching by Batch

1. First find the caller's old and current entries in the index; do not open a switch record until both are clearly identified.
2. Create or complete a migration batch for that caller, recording the old path, new path, and compatibility status separately. Each batch covers only confirmed samples.
3. Update the caller's status only after receiving integration feedback from the actual user. If the feedback concerns only one example or extension, update only that row's adaptation note.
4. Retain the old entry from before the switch for confirmed batches. The appearance of a new entry in the index only indicates that an alternative location exists; it cannot replace confirmation from the user.

This keeps both callers that are being migrated and callers that still require compatibility in the index, without letting one “migrated” entry conceal differences between batches.

## Reverting to the Old Entry

When a reversion is needed, locate the caller by migration batch first, then restore the old entry's usage status in that record; the directory state of the current entry cannot be used as the basis for the reversion. The reversion record should retain the compatibility status and integration feedback from that time, so the next switch does not treat the same adaptation issue as a new problem.

“Whether a reversion should restore only the old entry” has not been decided. Without confirmation, do not delete the current entry or mark compatible callers as complete. Once the caller's actual feedback is filled in, update the corresponding batch; implementation changes outside the index are not being pre-committed here.

```text
Is there an original failure record?
├─ No
│  ├─ Only a screenshot is available at this entry point: find the entry point and account used for the screenshot

```

There are only a few things to preserve first: the original input, version information from the time, the first visible failure, and whether `extension context` appeared. “First” here does not mean the earliest rerun. It means the material from when someone first saw the anomaly through this entry point. If all you have is a cleaned-up success report, stop here.

## Once the task is visible

Put the failure sample alongside the most recent normal sample and look only for the first difference. Don't start with averages, and don't use directory names to decide whether this belongs to the consumer or a shared component. If the first difference is still in the consumer fixture, hand it to the project maintainers. If the difference crosses a known interface, preserve the sample before handing it off. The handoff is not a request for the recipient to repeat the entire investigation; it carries over the one difference already observed.

```text
Where is the first difference?
├─ At this entry point or before report generation: check the entry-point material
├─ In the consumer fixture: continue within the project
├─ Beyond a clearly defined interface: hand off to the shared-component maintainers with the original sample
└─ Still cannot distinguish: do not assign a root cause
```

The old wording, “if there is no `Gradle task`, hand off to the permissions maintainers,” remains above, but is no longer sufficient. It conflates a collection gap with access denial. Only when access through the ordinary entry point is explicitly denied to a non-admin should the denial location and request/run id be recorded back on the original card. That is not a substitute for evidence of a test failure.

## Inputs that were rolled back

The original input after rollback was later confirmed, and the action associated with the new artifact was handled separately. This also changed the recovery sequence. Someone previously retried too early, leaving a green report but losing the first failure. # Troubleshooting Tree for Abnormal Handoffs from the Quality Signal Station

This page originally started as a short tree for cases where the “report did not appear.” Later, access issues, rolled-back inputs, and test-machine contention were all routed through the same entry point, so the tree was expanded over time. The old branches were not all removed: people still arrive here through old screenshots or old reports, and those materials retain the wording used at the time.

Do not rush to decide whom to contact. What the current entry point makes visible determines what can be done next; an image that contains only the final display is not enough to replace the original failure record.

```text
Start from the current entry point
│
├─ No test report
│  ├─ Screenshot only
│  │  ├─ Can recover the entry point and account used for the screenshot: restore this part of the evidence
│  │  └─ Cannot recover them: use the screenshot only as corroborating evidence, and stop assigning a cause
│  └─ Neither screenshot nor report: preserve the original input and collect the missing evidence first
│
└─ Test report exists
   ├─ No original failure sample: do not treat the rerun result as the original incident
   └─ Original failure sample exists
      ├─ Gradle task is visible: compare the first difference
      └─ Gradle task is not visible: return to the entry point for verification; do not jump to the permissions branch
```

At a minimum, the original failure sample here should let the person taking over see three things: the original input used at the time, the first visible failure, and whether the environment differed from the latest known-good sample. Whether `extension context` appears or does not appear must also be shown alongside these three items. By itself, it is only a location in the report; seeing it does not mean that the consumer fixture has been located, still less that an issue outside the interface has been established.

## How to handle the old entry point

The first version said: after finding `test report`, check `extension context`; stop if `Gradle task` does not appear. If the sample differed within the consumer fixture, contact the in-project maintainer. This section was useful in the original incident because the recovery action in the shared environment had not yet been tried.

Later, someone directly interpreted “the task did not appear” as an access or permissions issue. That interpretation remains in the old records, but now the first question should be where the report came from. Being denied at the standard entry point while using a non-administrator identity and having no task in the report are two different phenomena: the former requires recording where the denial occurred and the request/run id, while the latter primarily lacks material in the report chain. When both occur at the same time, one explanation still cannot be used to cover the other.

```text
Denied at the standard entry point?
├─ Yes: record the denial location and request/run id, then hand it off to the permissions maintainer
└─ No: do not attribute the missing task to permissions; continue checking the report entry point
```

This access branch handles denial at the standard entry point only. It does not vouch for the consumer’s test result or replace the failure sample. JEXB-018 record the entry point for this access attempt and are suitable for attaching the denial location; if what you received is a screenshot from an administrator’s perspective, return to the standard entry point for confirmation rather than mixing the two identities’ views into one conclusion.

## When a failure sample already exists

Place the sample next to the latest known-good sample and start only from the first difference. This restriction prevents inferring the process from directory names, summary numbers, or the final display. There is no need to provide a complete attribution before comparing them; confirming where the difference is already suffices to determine the handoff point for this round.

```text
First difference
├─ Before the current entry point
│  └─ Recheck the entry-point materials; do not hand it off to the consumer fixture
├─ Between the report and the Gradle task
│  └─ Retain the report and first failure, and continue checking adjacent tasks
├─ Within the consumer fixture
│  └─ Hand it over to the in-project maintainer
├─ Clearly across an interface
│  └─ Attach the original sample and difference location, and hand it off to the shared maintainer
└─ Still cannot be determined
   └─ Stop at the sample; do not specify a root cause
```

“Clearly across an interface” is a stopping point here, not a judgment about an external component. When handing it off, it is enough to include the original input, version information, the first failure, and the location of the first difference. Do not treat a later green report as proof of a fix; at most, it shows that another run did not reproduce the issue. The old records contain one premature retry: because the rerun came first, the first failure was not retained, and the process could later only be guessed from theorganizemanageafterofconclusionresult.

If the difference is still within the consumer fixture, do not therefore keep all subsequent actions on this page. This page is responsible only for sending the incident to the appropriate place. Specific fixture changes, interface adjustments, or new compatibility judgments should be documented by the receiving team in its own records.

## Do not merge materials from after a rollback

JEXB-007 was previously blocked because the caller had no failure sample. The original input was later rolled back, but the due action still pointed to the new artifact; the rolled-back original input was confirmed, and the action for the new artifact was handled separately. This sequence makes the old report look as if the same issue had two contradictory states, but in reality they are two separate evidence tracks.

When handling similar records, first ask which track the report corresponds to:

- If it corresponds to the original input before the rollback, investigate using the failure sample retained for that input;
- If it corresponds to the original input confirmed after the rollback, do not move the new artifact’s pending work back;
- If it corresponds to the new artifact, start a separate record and do not use the old input’s success or failure to draw a conclusion for it.

This section was added later; the first version did not contain this information. The old tendency to treat “green after a retry” as a recovery clue is now outdated; it is retained to explain why the process was later changed to retain the first failure sample first. This does not mean that every rollback produces a new artifact, nor that every report can be identified from its version text alone.

## Several places where work actually stopped

JEXB-006 originally intended to trace back from the current entry point and add the last confirmable state before the failure, but was later canceled because an existing ticket was already tracking the same issue. This ticket can help confirm the boundary of the old materials, but canceling it does not mean that the entry point has recovered, nor that the screenshot from that time has acquired a source.

JEXB-012 correspond to a screenshot with no source. If the entry point and account that generated the screenshot can be recovered, add them beside the failure sample; if not, explicitly retain it as corroborating evidence. Do not use a source-less screenshot to compare whether `extension context` is present, because it is impossible to confirm which run it came from.

JEXB-013 are the actual-use verification for the current revision: ask the party actually using it to follow the original entry point until the first difference. This was previously blocked because the test machine was occupied by another regression run. When the machine is unavailable, the result of another regression run cannot be used to replace this verification; you can save the existing samples first and wait for an opportunity to confirm from the original entry point.

JEXB-019 are suitable for a review by someone other than the author. The reviewer should follow the original steps, using the original author’s result only for comparison. If a new difference appears during the review, do not backfill it as if it had already existed in the old sample; record it separately to avoid mixing the two observations.

## Minimum package before handoff

When handing off from here, there is no need to organize a complete postmortem. It is enough to put the following materials together:

1. The address of the current entry point, or instructions that can locate it;
2. The original input and whether it has already been rolled back;
3. The first failure sample, or an explicit statement that it is missing;
4. The portions actually seen in `test report`, `Gradle task`, and `extension context`;
5. The first difference compared with the latest known-good sample;
6. If this was a denial at the standard entry point, the denial location and request/run id.

If any one item is missing, do not fill it in with guesses. In particular, when the original record is missing, the handoff content should say “collection pending,” not “suspected consumer issue.” This also explains why the early tree stopped at the first place where new evidence was needed: continuing to branch downward would create a handoff that looked clear but was not actually supported by a sample.

## Exits that are still available

- Failure occurred within the consumer fixture: the in-project maintainer continues.
- It is clear that the interface was crossed: hand off the minimum package to the shared maintainer.
- The standard entry point was explicitly denied: hand it off to the permissions maintainer and retain the denial location.
- It is still unclear whether the current revision was actually used: follow the original entry point in JEXB-013 to find the actual user.
- Only a screenshot, a green rerun, or a summary display is available: supplement the materials first; do not assign a root cause.

The handoff entry point remains `docs/adj-junit5-gradle-consumer/runbooks/junit5-gradle-consumer-quality-signal-Who to hand off to after getting stuck.md`. This page preserves the troubleshooting sequence from the period described above; when new report structures or new recovery actions are involved, keep a separate record rather than writing the new conclusion back into the old sample.

A temporary handoff is a processing slot added when an exit action is nearing expiry. It handles the expired action and records whether it was handled or remains unhandled; it does not take over interpretation of junit5-gradle-consumer-quality-signal. Behavior issues still go back to the original owner. If the long-term assignee has not confirmed, the blank remains in the table.

A single request often includes a version identifier, the current revision, and a second result. Record these separately. When collection or execution of the current revision has not been confirmed, keep the status unknown; if only the final state remains, do not use it to fill in a run or read.

## Handoff Table

| Operational point | Temporary maintainer handles | Route to |
|---|---|---|
| Exit action expires | Handle the expired action and record its handling status | Stop here when no behavior assessment is involved |
| Behavior interpretation of `junit5-gradle-consumer-quality-signal` | Provide no interpretation or conclusion | Original owner |
| Long-term handoff for `module path` | Do not fill the blank with the temporary maintainer | Blank, pending confirmation |
| Whether the current revision has been collected or executed | Keep the status unknown | Pending confirmation items for JEXB-003 |

# Maven Entry Point Migration Index

This index was originally intended only to put old entry points alongside their replacement locations. Later, it became clear that it also needed to retain where consumers had moved. Dependency provenance, adoption scope, and exit responsibilities associated with license cannot be collapsed into a single “migrated” record just because a directory was reorganized: the provenance information may move, adopters may not have switched, and exit responsibilities may still remain with the old entry point.

The index file is still at `docs/adj-junit5-maven-consumer/migration/current-entry-point-old-entry-point-migration-index.md`. The descriptions below preserve the migration criteria used at the time and should not be read as documentation of the entry points in use today. Entries that can no longer be traced remain in their original positions and are marked as old records, rather than being filled in to produce a new set of examples that looks complete.

## Initial Classification

Early records treated `extension context` as the old entry point and the separately extracted `Gradle task` as a candidate replacement entry point. This judgment came from the different failure exit paths at the two locations: fields with the same names were similar, but the paths returned to consumers differed. Moving things based only on directory names at that point would have carried the dependency provenance description to the replacement location while leaving out callers still coming through the old entry point.

```text
Before migration
Consumer ──> extension context ──> Dependency provenance registration

After trial use
Consumer ──> Gradle task ────────> Dependency provenance registration
   │
   └──Still returns to extension context when the trial is rolled back
```

This diagram does not declare the two entry points equivalent. It only shows that a migration batch needs to record the old entry point, the trial entry point, and the consumer together. Records under the old entry point must distinguish at least three things: where dependencies come from, which adopters are still using them, and who handles things after exit. These three items may be completed in different batches; they cannot all be crossed off just because one has a replacement location.

## Records Kept During Migration

Find the actual consumers in the index first, then decide whether this batch can be moved. The appearance of `Gradle task` in the directory is not enough to prove that calls through the old entry point have disappeared. Likewise, the old entry point still being accessible does not mean the migration failed. Each batch should record only the consumers involved in that batch, the old entry point name, the replacement location, and the adoption scope to which the dependency provenance description it leaves behind belongs.

The approach at the time was to retain the old entry point's original description first, then move one known consumer to the candidate entry point. Migration records do not compress results for different consumers into one overall status. When one caller completes trial use, only its own row changes; other callers remain recorded under the old entry point. This makes it possible to distinguish “a replacement location exists” from “the caller has adopted it” when reviewing the records, without inferring the latter from the former.

`Scala sample` was once listed as a caller to investigate, but the original record did not confirm which entry point it used. This blank was not filled in. It remains one of the easiest places in the old index to mistake for a handled item: seeing an example name is not the same as finding a caller actually in use, nor does it establish that its exit responsibilities have been transferred.

## Old Rollback Agreement

If the trial entry point produces a failure exit path different from the original path, first move that consumer back to `extension context` and do not expand the migration batch further. Keep the rollback record with the consumer, rather than leaving only a “rolled back” note beside the replacement entry point. Otherwise, later checks will show only that the new entry point once existed, not which adopter returned to the old path.

The old entry point remains readable after rollback so that dependency provenance, adoption scope, and exit responsibilities have a reference location for comparison. This does not require all consumers to remain at the old entry point forever. The replacement location and callers' actual migrations need to be recorded separately: the replacement location may remain, while consumers that have returned continue to be handled through the old path.

Someone later added a rollback observation: when an inconsistency is encountered, return to the old entry point rather than pushing ahead just to complete the batch. This addition did not resolve the original question of “whether rollback only restores the old entry point,” so the index did not turn it into a definite rule. Before relying on this old agreement, check whether the consumer actually belongs to the batch recorded at the time.

## Retained Old Entries

This index still retains the early description of `Gradle task` as the main replacement entry point. It reflects the comparison made at the time and does not cover other locations that may have appeared later. Old entry points, replacement locations, or callers whose versions cannot be checked remain unconfirmed; do not replace them with new names just to make the index look tidy.

Migration completion is not determined solely by whether one path turns green. Keeping separate records for the old entry point, the replacement location, and compatible callers makes it possible to find the original reference location when exit responsibilities have not yet been handed over.

# Package Integration Exit-Window Checklist

The previous draft rendered `Ant target`, `compatibility window` and `rollback check` as three very short gate terms. That wording was intended to prevent the live evidence from being cleared immediately after the window ended; it did not say what to retain when the records on the two sides diverged, and it did not distinguish “seeing the window” from “being able to close the window.”

This pass still covers only the exit action for builder-orchestration-package-integration, the last visible result, and the exit action for adj-builder-orchestration. This checklist does not determine whether the release succeeded; the responsible maintainer signs off separately. The checklist entry remains at:

`docs/adj-builder-orchestration/release/builder-orchestration-package-integration-exit-window-checklist.md`

The entry file is an artifact maintained by this project. Before opening the window, retrieve the current content referenced by that file and save it together with this input and the first visible result. Do not extract only one green result, and do not replace the state seen first with output organized later.

## Window-opening record

- [ ] Write down the revisions on the two sides to compare this time: builder-orchestration-package-integration. The task of JEXD-003 is to pin down this input set and compare only the revisions on these two sides; do not put other package combinations into the same comparison round.
- [ ] Compare the generation commands and times for the two instances of Builder and updater orchestration · Package integration collaboration. JEXD-006 requires stopping at the first divergence, so the record should start at the first inconsistency rather than append a speculative reason at the end.
- [ ] Export the state once before and once after the failure. JEXD-008 leaves the instruction “after reaching the current entry, first export the state before and after the failure”; these exports preserve the evidence and do not prove that recovery has succeeded.
- [ ] If `Ant target` is used as an anchor, state alongside it which input and which visible result it corresponds to. It is not a completion marker.

“Last visible result” means the last result that can be seen directly within the window; it is not the same as a “success” that appeared once in the logs. The previous draft did not distinguish these two things. Subsequent checks use the result saved from the live evidence.

## Handling after a divergence

JEXD-003 covers cases where the execution records match, but the stretch of timeline between that match and “the two sides’ builder-orchestr revisions do not match” is empty. When this combination occurs, do not infer the actions that took place in between merely from whether the generated results are the same or different.

1. Stop at the first confirmed divergence, and retain the revisions on both sides, the generation commands, the times, and the exported state.
2. Mark the timeline gap in the window record. The gap is not a failure cause that the maintainer may fill in independently.
3. Do not clear the original input, overwrite the state from before the failure, or write a result obtained later back into the first observation.
4. If `rollback check` is not in the entry materials or the live evidence, stop closing the window. The recovery action has not left a usable actual record; do not ad hoc treat guessed steps as a rollback plan.

`compatibility window` can still serve as an indication that the window has been identified, but it does not itself lift the stop point above. In particular, when the revisions already differ and the intermediate process has not been recorded, continuing cleanup after seeing this indication only removes the basis for later comparison.

## Window-closing actions

Proceed with the following closeout only when the window-opening record has no divergence, or when the live evidence has been retained at the stop point described above:

- [ ] Verify that the exit actions already performed match this run’s entry.
- [ ] Verify that the last visible result can still be matched to the saved input.
- [ ] Keep incomplete recovery items marked as incomplete; do not write them as a verified rollback.
- [ ] Hand the release sign-off to the responsible maintainer; this checklist does not replace that sign-off.

If any item cannot be verified, do not announce that the window is closed. Record only which action it stopped at, which state or timeline segment is missing; do not replace a specific incomplete item with “the project team will continue to monitor.”

This revision also leaves one misreading from the previous draft here: after seeing `compatibility window`, it previously required only “do not clear the evidence,” but did not require saving both revisions and the first divergence. Now fix the comparison objects first, then decide whether to proceed with the window-closing actions. The handling when `rollback check` is missing has not changed: stop rather than attempt unverified recovery.

Related entry points can be found through JEXD-003, JEXD-006, and JEXD-008; the three cards correspond respectively to revision comparison, the first divergence in generation commands and times, and retaining the state before and after failure. # Migration Freeze Decision Record

The initial draft compressed this freeze into “the entrypoint stays unchanged; the window can be discussed later.” That phrasing was easy to repeat, but it caused people reviewing the record later to conflate several different issues: whether the existing entrypoint remained within this round’s change scope, whether the window adjustment had been approved, and how to explain the change to callers when the capacity change actually occurred. The review did not overturn the decision to retain the entrypoint; it simply restated the boundaries that applied at the time.

This records the position for that migration train freeze, not a general rule for all migration trains that followed. Earlier, discussion leads were searched for using `junit5-mockito-extension/src/test/java/com/example/mockito/YourType.java` and the invocation name; that location was only the starting point for the search at the time and cannot be used to conclude that the maintenance boundary for bazel-integration has always been near that file.

## The Two Options on the Table

Northstar Build Systems presented only a few options during the freeze review.

One was to retain the current bazel-integration entrypoint. The direct implication was that people already depending on this entrypoint would not face an approved entrypoint replacement again at freeze time. This narrowed the change scope for the round and avoided changing both the entrypoint and the arrangements at the freeze point. However, retaining the entrypoint does not mean that the migration status of all callers has been confirmed. The entrypoint is only one object; it cannot vouch for the window, notifications, or future migration guidance.

The other was to adjust the migration train window. This was not about adding a note to the existing entrypoint; it could change when the build capacity change was announced and who would handle contact if a rollback occurred. The meeting did not treat the window as a purely scheduling detail. The source wording in the materials was:

> Build capacity changes are announced with a time window and a rollback contact.

At the time, this was treated as a condition for announcing a capacity change. The time window states when callers will begin to perceive the change; the rollback contact is the point of contact available if the change is rolled back or a problem occurs. They are listed together and cannot be handled by announcing one first and treating the other as a note to be filled in later.

This round ultimately chose the first option: retain the current bazel-integration entrypoint. The window adjustment was not approved with the freeze. The initial draft said “discuss it later,” which could easily be misread as meaning that it had already been scheduled for the next arrangement; the existing materials do not support that inference, so the wording is narrowed here to “not approved with this round.”

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[migration train freeze] --> B{Choices under review}
    B --> C[Retain the current bazel-integration entrypoint]
    B --> D[Adjust the migration train window]
    C --> E[Approved this round]
    D --> F[Not approved this round]
    G[Build metadata and migration notes disagree] --> H[Runnable example entrypoints and output visible to callersFang Ke]
    H --> I[Basis for the entrypoint decision]
```

The two branches in the diagram cannot be merged into “the freeze remains unchanged.” That wording may seem convenient, but it actually erases the difference in approval status: retaining the entrypoint was a decision that was made, while the window adjustment simply did not enter this round’s approval scope. The requirement for announcing a capacity change remains a condition that must accompany any capacity change proposed in the future; it does not automatically become invalid because the window did not pass.

## Why the Window Was Not Carried Along at the Time

The window proposal was not recorded as an explicit rejection. The reason for opposing it was also not that “the window adjustment is useless,” but that the materials did not explain how the adjustment would be communicated to callers together with retaining the existing entrypoint. If the two items were bound together in a single freeze decision, readers could easily assume that because the entrypoint remained, the arrangements on the caller side also remained exactly as they were; the review did not accept that extension.

The benefit of retaining the entrypoint was that it did not expand the scope of changes at freeze time. It introduced no new entrypoint replacement and did not require all migration paths to be re-explained at the same point. The cost was that the old entrypoint would still encourage people to rely on their existing understanding. Once the build metadata and migration notes diverge, the fact that “the entrypoint is still mentioned” alone cannot determine whether callers can still use it.

The cost of adjusting the window was different. It would affect the arrangements for announcing a capacity change. Even if no specific window was recorded, that does not allow the window change to be written off as internal scheduling that requires no explanation to callers. The meeting materials already placed the time window and rollback contact together; this shows that they were not two separable pieces of decorative information at the time.

A broader formulation was considered: since the entrypoint was not being changed, treat the window as unchanged as well and record this freeze as “status quo.” This was not adopted. It would miswrite “no new action was approved” as “the current state was confirmed to have nothing that needed explanation.” Another formulation took the opposite approach: as long as the migration notes still listed the entrypoint, treat the entrypoint as having been proven usable by the text. This was also not adopted because the notes and build metadata could contradict each other.

## Trade-Offs When a Conflict Occurs

The key judgment restored after the review was not to find a longer migration note, but to clarify the trade-off when the two types of material conflict. The meeting adopted the following:

> Use runnable example entrypoints and caller-visible output as the authority when build metadata and migration notes disagree.

The scope of this statement is narrow. It addresses only the dispute over whether an entrypoint can still serve as the basis for a decision when build metadata and migration notes disagree. In this type of conflict, runnable example entrypoints and the output visible to callers take precedence over two pieces of text that merely corroborate each other. This does not mean that every migration train issue requires running an entrypoint only once, nor does it turn entrypoint output into proof of a capacity window.

The initial draft did not spell out this distinction, leaving an inaccurate impression that build metadata, migration notes, and the existence of the entrypoint could be treated as the same kind of support. That impression should be withdrawn. Metadata can describe the expected path, and notes can describe the migration arrangements; but when they conflict, the simultaneous existence of both texts cannot prove where callers can actually get to.

“caller-visible output” here does not mean the target name in the build description either. It refers to the result that callers can actually see after invoking the entrypoint. The review adopted this point to avoid treating a seemingly complete explanation as behavior that had already occurred. Conversely, a runnable example entrypoint cannot provide a time range or rollback contact for a window adjustment.

Therefore, the approval scope for this round was deliberately limited to what the existing evidence could cover. This limitation is not intended to reject a broader migration narrative; it is intended to prevent the broader narrative from being written as a conclusion first and an entrypoint then being sought to fill it out. The judgment about retaining the entrypoint and the judgment about adjusting the window must each apply to their respective objects.

## Several Closing Formulations That Were Not Adopted

The first closing formulation that was not adopted was to write “retain the entrypoint,” “do not adjust the window for now,” and “capacity changes require notification” as one completed status. That would make it impossible for later readers to distinguish which item had been decided, which had not passed, and which was merely a requirement triggered when a capacity change was proposed in the future. The freeze decision did not assign the same status to these three items.

The second closing formulation that was not adopted was to provide a window first and add the rollback contact later. The meeting materials listed the two items together; the contact cannot be downgraded to an administrative add-on. There is no specific window or specific contact here; this record should not invent either one.

The third closing formulation that was not adopted was to treat the migration notes as the primary basis and then use the build metadata for confirmation. The problem was not that the notes had no reference value, but that this approach provided no way to adjudicate the matter after a conflict arose. The review chose runnable example entrypoints and caller-visible output precisely to preserve, in that kind of disagreement, a decision point close to caller behavior.

There was also a more aggressive proposal to eliminate the ambiguity caused by the old understanding by replacing the entrypoint. It did not enter this round’s selection. The decision at freeze time was not to reset the entrypoint, but to retain the current entrypoint without expanding the change scope. This decision reduced immediate change, but did not claim that material conflicts would never arise in the future.

## Addendum to the Initial Draft

“Leave the entrypoint unchanged” in the initial draft remains as a description of the result, but it should be read as “retain the current bazel-integration entrypoint for this round.” It is not a long-term ownership statement or a commitment to a subsequent replacement plan.

“Discuss the window later” from the initial draft is no longer used as the conclusion. The more accurate wording is: the window adjustment was not approved with this round’s freeze. The difference is material. The former implies that a subsequent point in time had already been assumed; the latter only states the approval status at the time. No material supports deriving the next window, the next review, or a definite execution order from this.

The initial draft also treated the explanation of the capacity change too lightly, as though it were an incidental note about the window issue. The original judgment remains in this addendum: whenever there is a build capacity change, the announcement must include both a time window and a rollback contact. The rollback here refers only to the rollback contact arrangement for that capacity change, not to a separate replacement guarantee for the bazel-integration entrypoint.

The reservation also remains. The window adjustment has not been shown to be infeasible; it simply did not receive this freeze’s approval. If it is proposed again later, it cannot contain only a time range; at minimum, it must also state the conditions for announcing the capacity change. At the same time, although retaining the entrypoint is a definite action, it must not be rewritten as the conclusion that “all callers have completed migration.”

DOC-44 contains a handoff record for shared CI maintenance. It can be used to look for handoff leads, but a contact not written in this decision must not be inferred to have been determined. This records the options and trade-offs at freeze time; it does not add another maintenance handoff.

## Archived Conclusion

The decision for this freeze remains to retain the current bazel-integration entrypoint. The window adjustment was not approved with it. If a build capacity change is proposed, the time window and rollback contact must be announced together.

When the build metadata and migration notes disagree, the entrypoint decision should use runnable example entrypoints and caller-visible output. This judgment supports only the entrypoint scope covered by the existing materials; it does not replace approval of the window adjustment or automatically turn the old notes into a result confirmed by callers.

# Migration Freeze Window Deviation Postmortem

This record covers a deviation during the migration train freeze window. The visible result during the window did not match the original plan. When it was first detected, we could only confirm that “an inconsistency occurred”; the inconsistency alone did not establish the cause. The original plan remains in the contemporaneous record. It can help compare against expectations, but it cannot substitute for the actual result.

## Timeline

- During the freeze window, we first found that the actual visible result had not appeared as originally planned.
- The initial detection and the recovery action were then recorded separately. Initial detection indicates when the deviation came to the on-call team’s attention; it must not be written as though the root cause had already been determined.
- The consumer reproduction retained the portion of the behavior that could be reproduced at the time. It proves that the consumer could see the same deviation, but it does not narrow the cause to a particular implementation or change.
- A temporary recovery was applied, allowing the window to continue processing. After recovery, the result returned to a state that could continue to be observed; this does not mean the original plan had been fully validated.

## Impact Assessment

The impact was primarily on decisions and progress during the freeze window. When the visible result does not match the plan, “should have appeared according to the plan” cannot be treated as “has appeared,” and the deviation cannot be marked as explained based only on the temporary recovery. The consumer reproduction showed that the issue was more than a discrepancy in internal records, but the available material does not define a more detailed impact scope, so this record does not extend it to unconfirmed callers or release results.

At the time, the cause was not narrowed to a single conclusion. The temporary recovery cleared the immediate blocker. What remains unknown is why this deviation appeared during the freeze window and which part between the original plan and the actual result failed to align. The recovery time must not be rewritten as the point when the root cause was already known.

## Controls Added Later

The record later added a coordination constraint: `Build capacity changes are announced with a time window and a rollback contact.` This requirement covers change notifications and the rollback entry point within the window. It can help the next on-call person know earlier when capacity changes may occur and find the rollback contact point if the result deviates again; it is not a retrospective explanation of the unknown cause in this incident.

Only two layers of assessment should remain: the deviation was detected during the freeze window, and a temporary recovery occurred; the cause was not confirmed along with the recovery. If this old record is changed later, the addition should be verifiable on-site results, not a more complete conclusion that overwrites what was unknown at the time.
